newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open weak before durables, jobless.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open weak before durables, jobless.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened weaker Thursday ahead of government reports on January durable goods orders and weekly jobless claims.
The benchmark 6-1/2 percent 30-year Treasury bond was off 4/32 to 97-31/32, yielding 6.78 percent.
The early weakness came after the market finished sharply lower Wednesday, taken aback by the hawkish tone of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony before Congress.

The market has a good helping of economic news on its plate today. At 0830 EST/1330 GMT the government will release data on durable goods orders for January. Orders are expected to be up 1.5 percent, according to economists polled by Reuters, after a 1.9 percent drop in December. Without defense-related goods, orders are expected to be up 2.2 percent after a 1.8 percent December decline.

Data on new jobless claims will also come out at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. New claims are expected to total 310,000 for the week ended February 22, little changed from the 309,000 new claims for unemployment insurance filed a week earlier.

Besides these two major economic reports, the market will get a purchasing managers report for the New York region at 0900 EST/1400 GMT. That index stood at 61.9 in January. No February forecast was available.

The 1000 EST/1500 GMT release of the Conference Board's January Help Wanted Advertising Index should attract some passing attention. It is expected to add to mounting evidence of a tight labor market.
The February APICS business outlook survey is also due at mid-morning. In January the index measured 45.9. No February forecast was available.
Analysts appeared divided on the market's likely course on Thursday.
"Technicals suggest further losses, although the market is due for a correction which would keep a positive tone today," said analysts at MMS International.
Economists agreed that the market's retreat on Wednesday was appropriate, given the consistently cautionary tone of Greenspan's remarks on Wednesday.
But Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, said the market could "crawl back a little bit" today.
"We've discounted enough of this (potential for monetary policy tightening)," said Rupkey.

"Your average dealer does not expect a tightening at the March FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting," he said. "Greenspan's testimony was a warning and it sounded pretty strong, but there's no imminent tightening. What are you going to do? Torture yourself with his warnings for a month?"
At the short end of the maturity curve, three-month bill rates were up one basis point to 5.06 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.09 percent.
Year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.32 percent.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-21/32, yielding 6.06 percent.
